studies.Title: Dietary patterns and risk of advanced prostate cancer: a principal component analysis in Uruguay.
studies.Reference: Dietary patterns and risk of advanced prostate cancer: a principal component analysis in Uruguay.
studies.Population: Uruguayan men newly diagnosed with advanced prostate cancer and hospitalized controls
studies.comparison_type: high quartile versus low quartile of the Western diet

extraction_supporting_text.sample_size: In order to explore the role of broader eating patterns in the etiology of prostate cancer, we conducted a principal components analysis among Uruguayan men. The study included 345 newly diagnosed cases of advanced prostate cancer and 690 hospitalized controls.
extraction_supporting_text.cases: The study included 345 newly diagnosed cases of advanced prostate cancer and 690 hospitalized controls.
extraction_supporting_text.effect_size: Whereas the traditional and Western patterns were directly associated with risk of prostate cancer (OR for high quartile versus the low quartile of the Western diet was 2.35, 95% CI 1.44-3.85, p-value for trend < 0.0001), the prudent, drinker, and substituter patterns were not associated with risk of the disease.
extraction_supporting_text.confidence_interval: Whereas the traditional and Western patterns were directly associated with risk of prostate cancer (OR for high quartile versus the low quartile of the Western diet was 2.35, 95% CI 1.44-3.85, p-value for trend < 0.0001), the prudent, drinker, and substituter patterns were not associated with risk of the disease.
extraction_supporting_text.comparison: high quartile versus the low quartile of the Western diet
extraction_supporting_text.timing: 345 newly diagnosed cases of advanced prostate cancer and 690 hospitalized controls
extraction_supporting_text.continent: the high incidence of advanced prostate cancer in Uruguay
extraction_supporting_text.location: a principal component analysis in Uruguay
extraction_supporting_text.exposure_measurement: The factor analysis was performed using the control population. Factor analysis allowed the extraction of five patterns, labeled as prudent, traditional, substituter, drinker, and Western.

sample_size.excerpt: A total of 43,469 men who participated in the Japan Public Health Center-based Prospective Study were followed from 1995 to 1998 to the end of 2012, during which 1,156 cases of prostate cancer were newly identified.

effect_size.excerpt: The westernized dietary pattern was associated with a higher risk of total prostate cancer (HR: 1.22; 95% CI 1.00-1.49; p trend = 0.021), localized cancer (HR: 1.24; 95% CI 0.97-1.57; p trend = 0.045), and advanced cancer (HR: 1.23; 95% CI 0.82-1.84; p trend = 0.233).

confidence_interval.excerpt: The westernized dietary pattern was associated with a higher risk of total prostate cancer (HR: 1.22; 95% CI 1.00-1.49; p trend = 0.021), localized cancer (HR: 1.24; 95% CI 0.97-1.57; p trend = 0.045), and advanced cancer (HR: 1.23; 95% CI 0.82-1.84; p trend = 0.233).

p_value.excerpt: The westernized dietary pattern was associated with a higher risk of total prostate cancer (HR: 1.22; 95% CI 1.00-1.49; p trend = 0.021)

headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an overall effect size of 1.35 (95% CI: 1.0–1.82), suggesting that western pattern diet is associated with a higher risk of prostate cancer. However, this association should be interpreted with caution, as there was substantial between-study heterogeneity (I² = 57.15%), reflecting considerable variability across studies.
